title: The scientific method; hypothesis, theory and law
blurb: Put the steps of the scientific method in order, write a testable hypothesis, and tell a hypothesis, theory, law, observation and inference apart.
question: A student notices that bread in her warm pantry grows mold faster than bread in the refrigerator. What should her next steps be, how should she word her hypothesis, and what can she claim if her results agree with it?

teach.body: Formally, the scientific method is a systematic process of making observations, forming testable hypotheses, testing them by experiment and drawing evidence-based conclusions. In plain English: notice something, ask why, make a guess you could prove wrong, test it fairly, and let the data decide. Real science loops back: a rejected hypothesis is revised and tested again, and results are shared so others can check them.

teach.loop: Hypothesis rejected? Revise it and test again
teach.caption: Ordered-response items often swap one adjacent pair, such as research and hypothesis. Research comes BEFORE the hypothesis.

teach.body: A hypothesis is a testable, tentative explanation or prediction, often written 'If ... then ... because ...'. It must be falsifiable: some possible result would show it is wrong. It is not a question ('Does light affect growth?'), not an opinion ('Roses are the prettiest flower') and not a plain observation ('The plant grew 4 cm').

rows.label: Does the amount of light affect bean plant growth?
Bean plants are the best plants for a classroom.
The bean plant by the window grew 4 cm in a week.
If bean plants get more hours of light, then they will grow taller, because light powers photosynthesis.

teach.note: Only the last one predicts an outcome that a fair test could contradict.

teach.caption: Both theories and laws can be revised if new evidence demands it. A model is a simplified representation (physical, mathematical or conceptual) used to explain and predict.

teach.text: A theory is NOT a guess, and it does NOT 'graduate' into a law once proven. Theories explain and laws describe: they do different jobs. Experiments also never 'prove' a hypothesis: data SUPPORT it or FAIL TO SUPPORT it.

head: Statement
Observation or inference
Data type
teach.caption: An observation is what you directly see or measure. An inference interprets observations. Qualitative data describe; quantitative data are numbers with units.

teach.body: A conclusion states whether the data support or fail to support the hypothesis, describes the relationship found, and notes limits and sources of error. Supporting data never prove a hypothesis, but one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it. Scientists then communicate results so others can replicate them, and peer review checks the methods and conclusions before publication.

children.label: Hypothesis not supported
children.sub: Revise it and design a new test

teach.h: Scenario: Priya and the moldy bread
teach.body: Priya, a pre-nursing student, OBSERVES that bread molds faster in her warm pantry. She ASKS whether temperature affects mold growth and RESEARCHES how microorganisms grow. HYPOTHESIS: if bread is stored warmer, then mold will appear sooner, because microorganisms grow faster in warmth. She EXPERIMENTS with identical slices at 4 °C, 20 °C and 30 °C, ANALYZES days to visible mold, and CONCLUDES her data support the hypothesis. She shares her method so classmates can repeat it.

items: Order: observe, question, research, hypothesis, experiment, analyze data, conclude, communicate.
A hypothesis is testable and falsifiable, often 'If ... then ... because ...'.
Theory: broad, well-tested explanation (why). Law: description of what happens, often mathematical.
Theories do not become laws, and a theory is not a guess.
Data support or fail to support a hypothesis; they never prove it.
Observation = seen or measured; inference = interpretation. Qualitative = descriptive; quantitative = numbers.

summary: You can now order the steps of the scientific method, recognize a testable hypothesis and tell it apart from a question, opinion or observation. You can also distinguish theories from laws and observations from inferences, and state a conclusion without claiming proof.

A.q: A scientist has just written a hypothesis. Which step of the scientific method normally comes next?
options: Research what is already known
Draw a conclusion from the data
Test it with an experiment
Publish the results for review
A.why: After forming a hypothesis, the scientist designs and conducts an experiment to test it.

whyNot.0: Background research comes BEFORE the hypothesis, so the hypothesis is informed.
whyNot.1: There are no data to conclude from until the experiment has been run.
whyNot.3: Results are communicated at the end, after data analysis and a conclusion.

A.q: Which statement is a testable hypothesis?
options: Does the amount of light affect how tall bean plants grow?
If bean plants get more light, then they will grow taller
Bean plants are the most attractive plants to grow indoors
Bean plants grew 4 cm taller in the sunny window last week
A.why: An 'If ... then ...' statement predicts a measurable outcome that an experiment could support or contradict.

whyNot.0: This is a research question. A hypothesis proposes an answer to it.
whyNot.2: This is an opinion; 'attractive' cannot be tested objectively.
whyNot.3: This is an observation of what already happened, not a testable prediction.

A.q: Which statement about scientific theories and laws is CORRECT?
options: A theory becomes a law once it is proven
A law explains why; a theory describes what happens
A theory is an educated guess awaiting a first test
A theory explains why; a law describes what happens
A.why: A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of why things happen; a law describes what consistently happens, often as a formula, without explaining why.

whyNot.0: Theories never 'graduate' into laws; they do different jobs.
whyNot.2: An untested guess is closer to a hypothesis. A theory is supported by extensive evidence.

B.q: A student records four statements about a wilted houseplant. Which is an INFERENCE?
options: The leaves droop and are brown at the tips
The soil is dry 3 cm below the surface
The plant has not been watered enough
The stem measures 14 cm from soil to tip
B.why: Concluding that the plant lacks water interprets the observations; it is not directly seen.

whyNot.0: Drooping, brown leaves are directly observed.
whyNot.1: Dry soil is an observation made by touch or with a probe.
whyNot.3: A length measured with a ruler is a quantitative observation.

B.q: Which result from a chemistry lab is QUANTITATIVE data?
options: The solution turned a cloudy pink
The gas smelled like rotten eggs
The crystals formed fine needles
The solution reached pH 8.2
B.why: Quantitative data are numerical measurements; a pH reading of 8.2 is a number.

whyNot.0: Color and cloudiness are descriptions: qualitative data.
whyNot.2: Crystal shape is described in words, so it is qualitative.

B.q: The results of a well-designed experiment do not support a researcher's hypothesis. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Revise the hypothesis and test it again
Discard the results as experimental error
Change the conclusion to match the hypothesis
Add a second independent variable and retest
B.why: The scientific method is iterative: a hypothesis that is not supported is revised (or replaced) and tested again.

whyNot.1: Unwelcome data from a well-designed test are still evidence; they cannot be dismissed without a real flaw.
whyNot.2: A conclusion must follow the data, not the researcher's expectation.
whyNot.3: Changing two variables at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any effect.

C.q: Kayla hypothesizes that if seeds are soaked overnight, then they will sprout sooner. In three trials, soaked seeds sprouted 2 days earlier than unsoaked seeds. Which conclusion is BEST?
options: The data support the hypothesis
The data prove the hypothesis is true
The hypothesis has become a theory
The hypothesis has become a law
C.why: Results that agree with a hypothesis support it. Further evidence could still contradict it, so it is not proven.

whyNot.1: Experiments support or fail to support a hypothesis; they do not prove it.
whyNot.2: A theory is a broad explanation built on many lines of evidence, not one small study.
whyNot.3: Hypotheses and theories do not turn into laws; laws describe consistent patterns.

C.q: Which sequence places these steps of the scientific method in the correct order?
options: Question, hypothesis, research, experiment, conclusion
Question, research, experiment, hypothesis, conclusion
Question, research, hypothesis, conclusion, experiment
Question, research, hypothesis, experiment, conclusion
C.why: After the question, research informs the hypothesis; the experiment tests it; the conclusion comes from the data.

whyNot.0: Research and hypothesis are swapped: background research comes before the hypothesis.
whyNot.1: The hypothesis must be formed before the experiment that tests it.
whyNot.2: A conclusion cannot come before the experiment produces data.

C.q: Which statement is a scientific LAW rather than a theory?
options: In a closed system, total mass stays the same during a reaction
All living things are made of cells that come from existing cells
Many diseases are caused by microorganisms invading the body
Species change over many generations through natural selection
C.why: The law of conservation of mass describes what consistently happens to mass in a reaction without explaining why.

whyNot.1: This is cell theory, a broad explanation of how life is organized.
whyNot.2: This is germ theory, an explanation of the cause of infectious disease.
whyNot.3: This is the theory of evolution, an explanation of how species change over time.

reteach.title: The scientific method is how a detective works
reteach.question: A detective arrives at a scene, gathers clues, names a suspect and then checks the alibi. How does that match observation, hypothesis, experiment and conclusion?

blocks.body: The detective notices clues (observation), asks who did it (question) and checks the files (research). Naming a suspect is the hypothesis: it must be checkable, because the alibi might clear them. Testing the alibi is the experiment. If the alibi holds, the detective revises the theory of the case and tests a new suspect. A strong case is 'supported by the evidence', never beyond all future doubt.

blocks.text: A detective who ignores an alibi because they 'just know' who did it is not doing science. Conclusions follow the evidence, not the investigator's hopes.

explain.body: Observe, question, research, hypothesis, experiment, analyze data, conclude, communicate. If the hypothesis is not supported, revise it and test again.

test.q: Between asking a question and forming a hypothesis, a scientist usually:
options: draws a conclusion
collects and analyzes data
does background research
communicates the results
test.why: Background research on what is already known comes after the question and informs the hypothesis.

whyNot.0: A conclusion comes after the experiment and data analysis.
whyNot.1: Data are collected during the experiment, after the hypothesis.
whyNot.3: Communicating results is the final step.

explain.body: A testable, tentative explanation or prediction that could be shown false. 'If (I change this), then (this will happen), because (reason).' Not a question, opinion or observation.

test.q: A useful scientific hypothesis must be:
options: Testable and falsifiable
Written as an open question
Already supported by data
Agreed on by most experts
test.why: A hypothesis must be testable, and some possible result must be able to show it is wrong.

whyNot.1: A question prompts a hypothesis; the hypothesis proposes an answer.
whyNot.2: A hypothesis is tentative and is tested AFTER it is written.
whyNot.3: Agreement among experts is not evidence and is not required of a hypothesis.

explain.body: A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of many observations (cell theory, germ theory). A law describes what consistently happens, often mathematically (conservation of mass). A model is a simplified representation used to explain and predict.

test.q: A scientific theory is best described as:
options: an untested guess about a single result
a broad, well-tested explanation
a law that is still waiting for proof
a description of what happens, not why
test.why: A theory explains a wide range of observations and has been repeatedly tested and supported.

whyNot.0: An untested idea is a hypothesis, and a theory covers many observations.
whyNot.2: Theories do not turn into laws when 'proven'.
whyNot.3: Describing what happens without explaining why is the job of a law.

explain.body: Observations are what you directly see or measure; inferences interpret them. Qualitative data describe (color, smell, texture); quantitative data are numbers with units.

test.q: A lab technician records four facts about a urine sample. Which is QUALITATIVE data?
options: The sample's volume was 450 mL
The sample was pale yellow
The sample had a pH of 6.0
The sample's mass was 452 g
test.why: Color is a description in words, so it is qualitative data.

whyNot.0: A volume in mL is a number with a unit: quantitative.
whyNot.2: A pH value is a number: quantitative.
whyNot.3: A mass in grams is a number with a unit: quantitative.
